topics.title: Henry VIII and the Reformation
topics.intro: A king who wanted a son, a Pope who said no, and a country that changed its religion. The Reformation reshaped England’s churches, monasteries and politics for centuries.
topics.teach: Explain why Henry VIII broke with Rome. Was it really about religion?
topics.talk: Ask her the rhyme for the six wives: divorced, beheaded, died…
topics.hook: The three Hs of the break with Rome: an **heir** (a son), his **heart** (Anne Boleyn) and the Church’s **hoard** of wealth.

topics.title: Elizabeth I and the Spanish Armada
topics.intro: In 1588 the most powerful country in Europe sent 130 ships to invade England. It failed, thanks to fireships, fast English ships and the weather.
topics.teach: Explain three reasons the Armada failed.
topics.talk: Ask her why Philip II wanted to invade England in the first place.
topics.hook: “God blew and they were scattered”: the words on a medal struck after the Armada.

topics.title: The Stuarts and the Civil War
topics.intro: Within fifty years of Elizabeth’s death, England executed its king. The argument was about who ruled: the king alone, or the king with Parliament.
topics.teach: Explain the main causes of the English Civil War.
topics.talk: Ask her whether a country can put its own king on trial. What happened in 1649?
topics.hook: **Cavaliers** for the king, **Roundheads** for Parliament: war **1642**, king executed **1649**, king restored **1660**.

topics.title: Interpretations: why historians disagree
topics.intro: An interpretation is a historian’s view of the past, built from the evidence they have, for the audience they write for. Richard III has been a monster, a victim and a mystery, depending on who is telling the story.
topics.teach: Explain why two historians can look at the same evidence and disagree.
topics.talk: Ask her how a Tudor writer and a modern one might describe Richard III differently, and why.
topics.hook: “History is written by the winners”, so always ask **who** wrote it, **when**, and **why**.

items.prompt: Why did Henry VIII want to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon?

options.text: She had not given him a son
She had become a Protestant
options.feedback: Catherine was a devout Catholic. The problem was the lack of a male heir.

options.text: She had gone back to Spain
options.feedback: She stayed, and refused to accept the annulment.

items.explain: Henry believed England needed a male heir to avoid another civil war. Catherine had one surviving child, Mary.
items.hook: Henry’s father won the crown in battle: without a son, Henry feared another war over the throne.
items.example: Catherine of Aragon is buried in Peterborough Cathedral; visitors still leave pomegranates, her symbol, on her tomb.

items.prompt: Who refused to grant Henry VIII an annulment of his first marriage?
items.explain: Pope Clement VII refused, partly because Catherine’s nephew, Emperor Charles V, controlled Rome.
items.hook: Pope **Clement** was not “clement” (merciful) to Henry: he said no.

items.prompt: The Act of Supremacy (1534) made Henry VIII the…
items.answer: Supreme Head of the Church of England
items.explain: From 1534 the king, not the Pope, was head of the Church in England. Refusing to accept this was treason.
items.hook: **Supreme Head**: from 1534 the king sat at the top of the Church as well as the country.
items.example: The monarch still has the title “Supreme Governor of the Church of England”.

items.prompt: In which year was the Act of Supremacy passed?
items.explain: 1534: the formal break with Rome.
items.hook: Married Anne Boleyn in 15**33**, Supreme Head in 15**34**: one year after the other.

items.prompt: Which minister organised the closing (dissolution) of the monasteries for Henry VIII?
items.explain: Cromwell’s commissioners valued, closed and sold off about 800 monasteries between 1536 and 1540. The Crown took the land and wealth.
items.hook: Two Cromwells: **Thomas** for the Tudors (monasteries), **Oliver** a century later (Civil War).

items.prompt: Why did Henry close the monasteries?

options.text: For their wealth and their loyalty to Rome
Because nobody lived in them any more
options.feedback: Thousands of monks and nuns lived in them. They were turned out.

options.text: To turn them into hospitals and schools
options.feedback: A few became schools or cathedrals, but most of the money went to the Crown and its supporters.

items.explain: The dissolution made Henry rich and bought him the loyalty of the gentry who got the land. It also destroyed libraries, charity and ancient buildings.
items.hook: Monasteries = money: about 800 closed, their land sold or given to loyal gentry.
items.example: Grand houses such as Woburn Abbey stand on land taken from monasteries; they kept the name “abbey”.

items.prompt: Which former chancellor was executed in 1535 for refusing to accept Henry as head of the Church?
items.explain: More would not swear the oath. He was beheaded in 1535 and is now a Catholic saint.
items.hook: Thomas **More** would swear no **more**: he refused Henry’s oath.
items.example: More wrote “Utopia”: the word we still use for a perfect, imaginary place.

items.prompt: Put Henry VIII’s six wives in order.
items.explain: Divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived. Jane Seymour gave him his son, Edward.
items.hook: “Divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived.” Three Catherines, two Annes and one Jane.
items.example: Jane Seymour, mother of Edward VI, is buried beside Henry VIII in St George’s Chapel, Windsor.

items.prompt: Which of Henry’s three children made England most firmly Protestant?

options.text: Edward VI
Mary I
options.feedback: Mary restored Catholicism and burned about 280 Protestants, earning the name “Bloody Mary”.

options.text: Elizabeth I
options.feedback: Elizabeth found a middle way (the Religious Settlement of 1559). Edward’s reign was the most strongly Protestant.

items.explain: Edward VI (1547–53) brought in an English prayer book and plain churches. Mary swung back to Rome; Elizabeth settled on a Protestant church with some old ceremony.
items.hook: A religious see-saw: Edward **Protestant**, Mary **Catholic**, Elizabeth the **middle way**.
items.example: The English Book of Common Prayer began under Edward VI in 1549; versions are still used in churches.

items.prompt: Elizabeth I’s Religious Settlement of 1559 made her the “Supreme ___” of the Church of England.
items.explain: Not “Head”: Elizabeth chose the softer title Supreme Governor to reassure Catholics and those who objected to a woman heading the Church.
items.hook: Elizabeth chose **Governor**, not Head: a softer word to keep Catholics calm.
items.example: King Charles III still holds the title Supreme Governor of the Church of England.

items.prompt: In which year did the Spanish Armada sail against England?
items.explain: 1588. Elizabeth had been queen for thirty years.
items.hook: “Fifteen eighty-eight, the Spanish fleet met its fate.”

items.prompt: Which king of Spain sent the Armada?
items.explain: Philip II had been married to Mary I of England. He saw Protestant Elizabeth as a heretic and a threat.
items.hook: Philip II was Elizabeth’s **brother-in-law**: he had been married to her sister, Mary I.
items.example: The Philippines, in South-East Asia, are named after Philip II of Spain.

items.prompt: Which of these was NOT a reason Philip II attacked England?

options.text: England had invaded Spain
English sailors like Drake were raiding Spanish treasure ships
options.feedback: This was a real reason: Elizabeth quietly profited from Drake’s piracy.

options.text: Elizabeth had executed the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots in 1587
options.feedback: A real reason: Mary’s death removed the Catholic heir and enraged Philip.

items.explain: Religion (Catholic Spain against Protestant England), piracy, English help for Dutch rebels, and Mary’s execution all pushed Philip to invade. England had not invaded Spain, though Drake had raided Cadiz in 1587.
items.hook: Four Rs: **R**eligion, **R**aids on treasure ships, **R**ebels in the Netherlands helped by England, a **R**oyal execution.

items.prompt: Which English sea captain “singed the King of Spain’s beard” by raiding Cadiz in 1587?
items.explain: Drake destroyed ships and supplies at Cadiz, delaying the Armada by a year.
items.hook: “Singeing the King of Spain’s beard”: Drake’s cheeky raid on Cadiz delayed the Armada by a year.
items.example: Drake’s Drum, said in legend to beat when England is in danger, is kept at Buckland Abbey in Devon.

items.prompt: What did the English send into the anchored Armada at Calais at night?
items.explain: Eight burning ships drifted into the Spanish fleet. The Spanish cut their anchors and scattered, breaking their defensive crescent.
items.hook: **Fire**ships at night → panic → the Spanish cut their anchors and lost their crescent shape.

items.prompt: Where did the English fleet fight the scattered Armada the day after the fireships?
items.explain: At the Battle of Gravelines (8 August 1588) the faster English ships and longer-range guns did real damage.
items.hook: First **fire** at Calais, then the **fight** at Gravelines the next day.
items.example: Gravelines is a small town on the French coast between Calais and Dunkirk.

items.prompt: Why did so many Spanish ships sink on the way home?

options.text: They sailed home round Scotland, into storms
The English chased them all the way to Spain
options.feedback: The English ran low on ammunition and turned back. The storms did the rest.

options.text: They ran out of food and water and gave up
options.feedback: Food and water were short, but the ships were wrecked by weather on the Irish coast.

items.explain: The wind blew the Armada into the North Sea. Going home the long way, perhaps a third of the ships were lost. The English struck a medal: “God blew and they were scattered.”
items.hook: “God blew and they were scattered”: the words on England’s Armada medal.
items.example: Gold from the Armada ship Girona, wrecked off Northern Ireland, is on show in the Ulster Museum, Belfast.

items.prompt: How was news of the Armada’s approach spread quickly along the English coast?
items.explain: A chain of hilltop bonfires carried the warning from Cornwall to London in hours.
items.hook: Hill to hill, fire to fire: like passing a message down a line of friends.
items.example: Beacons are still lit on hilltops across Britain to celebrate royal jubilees.

items.prompt: Who commanded the Armada?
items.explain: Medina Sidonia was a nobleman with little experience at sea; he had begged Philip not to appoint him. Parma commanded the army waiting in the Netherlands that the Armada was supposed to collect.
items.hook: Medina Sidonia begged **not** to command: he had little experience at sea and said he suffered from seasickness.

items.prompt: Who became king of England when Elizabeth I died in 1603?
items.explain: James VI of Scotland became James I of England, uniting the two crowns.
items.hook: James **VI and I**: the sixth of Scotland, the first of England. One king, two numbers.
items.example: The King James Bible (1611), made in his reign, is still read today.

items.prompt: In which year did Guy Fawkes and the plotters try to blow up Parliament?
items.explain: The Gunpowder Plot, 5 November 1605: a group of Catholics planned to kill James I at the opening of Parliament.
items.hook: “Remember, remember the fifth of November, gunpowder, treason and plot.”
items.example: Before every State Opening of Parliament, guards still search the cellars because of the 1605 plot.

items.prompt: Which was a cause of the Civil War?

options.text: Charles ruled without Parliament for eleven years
Parliament wanted to make England Catholic again
options.feedback: Many MPs feared the opposite: that Charles and his Catholic queen were steering England back to Rome.

options.text: Charles I refused to collect any taxes at all
options.feedback: He collected them without Parliament’s permission, which was the problem.

items.explain: Money, religion and power: Charles believed in the Divine Right of Kings; Parliament believed the king must rule with it.
items.hook: **Money, religion, power**: and Charles ruled with no Parliament for 11 years (1629–40).

items.prompt: Charles I believed God had chosen him to rule and he answered to no one on earth. What is this idea called?
items.explain: Divine Right: the king is appointed by God, so opposing him is a sin. Parliament disagreed.
items.hook: **Divine** = from God: “God chose the king, so only God can judge him.”

items.prompt: In which year did the English Civil War begin?
items.explain: August 1642: Charles raised his standard at Nottingham after trying and failing to arrest five MPs in January.
items.hook: War **1642**, king executed **1649**: seven years from the first battle to the king’s trial.
items.example: Standard Hill, a street in Nottingham, is named after the spot where Charles raised his standard in 1642.

items.prompt: What nickname was given to the supporters of Parliament?
items.explain: Roundheads, from the short haircuts of London apprentices. The king’s supporters were Cavaliers.
items.hook: **Round**heads had short, round haircuts; **Cavaliers** (from an old word for horseman) wore long curls.

items.prompt: At which 1645 battle did Parliament’s New Model Army decisively defeat the king?
items.explain: Naseby, June 1645. The New Model Army was professional, well paid and led by ability rather than birth.
items.hook: **N** for **N**: **N**aseby was the **N**ew Model Army’s great win.

items.prompt: Which Parliamentary commander later ruled England as Lord Protector?
items.explain: Cromwell was Lord Protector from 1653 until his death in 1658. England had no king for eleven years.
items.hook: Cromwell refused the crown, but as **Lord Protector** he ruled almost like a king.
items.example: A statue of Oliver Cromwell stands outside the Houses of Parliament in London.

items.prompt: In which year was Charles I executed?
items.explain: 30 January 1649, outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall. The only English king ever tried and executed by his own people.
items.hook: ’42 war, ’49 execution, ’60 crown back: the Civil War years in a row.
items.example: The Banqueting House in Whitehall, outside which Charles I was executed, still stands; its ceiling was painted by Rubens.

items.prompt: Which event in 1660 brought Charles II to the throne?
items.explain: After Cromwell died, Parliament invited Charles I’s son back. The monarchy was restored, but it never again ruled without Parliament for long.
items.hook: **Re**storation = the king **re**stored, in **1660**, after 11 years with no king.
items.example: Charles II hid in an oak tree in 1651, which is why so many pubs are called the Royal Oak.

items.prompt: Put these Stuart events in order.
items.explain: Plot 1605, war 1642, Naseby 1645, execution 1649, Restoration 1660.
items.hook: All in the 1600s, so learn the endings: **05, 42, 45, 49, 60**.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a source and an interpretation?

options.text: A source is from the time; an interpretation is later
They are the same thing, with different names
options.feedback: A Tudor portrait is a source; a modern biography that uses it is an interpretation.

options.text: An interpretation is always more reliable than a source
options.feedback: Interpretations can be biased or outdated too. They depend on the evidence and the historian.

items.explain: Sources are raw material; interpretations are what historians, film-makers and textbook writers make from them.
items.hook: A **source** is a raw ingredient from the time; an **interpretation** is the meal a historian cooks later.

items.prompt: Two historians disagree about the same king. Which is the LEAST likely reason?

options.text: One of them is lying
They are writing for different audiences (a children’s book and an academic study)
options.feedback: A very common reason: purpose and audience shape what is emphasised.

options.text: New evidence has been found since the older one wrote
options.feedback: Also common: interpretations change as evidence changes.

items.explain: Historians usually differ because of evidence, purpose, audience and the times they live in, not dishonesty.
items.hook: Historians differ because of **evidence**, **purpose**, **audience** and their own **times**, not because they lie.

items.prompt: Shakespeare’s Richard III (about 1593) shows the king as a scheming, hunchbacked murderer. Why should a historian be cautious about this interpretation?

options.text: It was written under the Tudors, his enemies
Shakespeare never wrote about real people
options.feedback: He wrote many history plays, but as drama, not record.

options.text: Plays cannot contain any historical truth
options.feedback: They can. The point is to ask who wrote it, when, and for whom.

items.explain: Shakespeare drew on Tudor writers such as Thomas More. Under Elizabeth I, Henry VII’s granddaughter, there was every reason to blacken Richard.
items.hook: “History is written by the winners”, and the Tudors were the winners at Bosworth.
items.example: Shakespeare’s Richard III is still performed today, so his Tudor version of Richard is the one most people know.

items.prompt: In 2012 Richard III’s skeleton was found under a car park in Leicester. It showed a curved spine (scoliosis) but no withered arm. How does this affect interpretations?

options.text: It supports part of the Tudor picture but not all
It proves Shakespeare was right about everything
options.feedback: The curved spine matches; the withered arm and “hunchback” do not.

options.text: It proves that Richard was a good and fair king
options.feedback: Bones cannot tell us about his character or whether he killed the princes.

items.explain: New evidence rarely settles everything. It changes the balance, and interpretations shift with it.
items.hook: New evidence usually **nudges** an interpretation rather than knocking it down.
items.example: The King Richard III Visitor Centre in Leicester is built on the site where his skeleton was found.

items.prompt: When judging an interpretation, which three questions about its author matter most?
items.answer: who, when, and why they wrote it
distractors: how long it is, how old it is, how much it cost
whether it has pictures, maps and a glossary
whether it agrees with your own view
items.explain: Who made it (expertise and loyalties), when (what evidence existed) and why (purpose and audience) explain most disagreements.
items.hook: The three Ws: **W**ho, **W**hen and **W**hy.

items.prompt: A 1950s school textbook calls the British Empire “a great gift to the world”. A 2020 textbook stresses the harm it did. Which statement is fairest?

options.text: Both are shaped by their times; check the evidence
The newer one must be right because it is newer
options.feedback: Newer interpretations use more evidence and new perspectives, but they are still interpretations.

options.text: The older one must be right: it is closer in time
options.feedback: Being closer in time does not make a view neutral. Each generation sees the past through its own concerns.

items.explain: Interpretations tell you about the past AND about the time they were written in.
items.hook: Every interpretation has two dates: the date it is **about** and the date it was **written**.

items.prompt: A film shows a Roman soldier wearing a wristwatch. What is this mistake called?
items.explain: An anachronism is something placed in the wrong time period. Historians look out for them in films, novels and even in old history books.
items.hook: **Ana** = against, **chron** = time: something set against its proper time.
items.example: Shakespeare made one: in his play Julius Caesar a clock strikes, though the Romans had no striking clocks.
